Wednesday 9/23/2026 p.m.
Stocks fall with rising bond yields weighing on sentiment –
U.S. equity markets closed lower on Wednesday, as rising Treasury yields weighed on investor sentiment. The 10-year yield climbed to 5.11%, its highest level since 2007, with robust economic data, hawkish comments from Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr, and a poorly received Treasury auction likely all contributing to Wednesday’s rise in yields. From a leadership perspective, energy was the only S&P 500 sector to finish in positive territory, while rate-sensitive sectors such as utilities and real estate, along with growth-oriented sectors including communication services and consumer discretionary, were among the laggards. On the economic front, the September S&P Global U.S. Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) showed that business activity remained resilient, with the U.S. composite PMI rising to 58.4, its highest level in more than five years. While business activity remained robust, price pressures also appeared persistent, with input costs increasing across both the manufacturing and services sectors, likely contributing to the rise in bond yields. In commodity markets, oil prices finished modestly higher, with WTI crude closing near $93 per barrel and snapping a streak of five consecutive daily declines.
Global economic activity remains firm in September –
Wednesday brought an update on global economic trends with the preliminary September S&P Global Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) readings. PMIs measure business activity, with readings above 50 indicating expansion and readings below 50 indicating contraction. Overnight, the eurozone composite PMI rose to 53.1 in September, its highest level since April 2023, supported primarily by improvement in the services sector. Activity also continued to expand in the United Kingdom. Although the U.K. composite PMI declined modestly, it remained above 50 at 51.7. In the U.S., activity remained firm as well, with the composite PMI rising to 58.4, the highest level in over five years. For all three regions, the downside of the September data was persistent price pressure, as input costs increased amid higher oil prices. Against a backdrop of resilient business activity and persistent price pressure, global bond yields surged, with the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield climbing to 5.11%, while long-term bond yields in the United Kingdom and euro area were sharply higher on Wednesday as well. Despite the headwind of elevated yields and persistent price pressures, economic activity has proven resilient in 2026, helping support a 12% gain in international developed large-cap stocks and a 14% gain in the S&P 500 through yesterday’s close. We continue to see attractive opportunities in equity markets over the coming months, supported by resilient economic activity and strong profit growth.
Midterm elections and implications for investors –
Midterm Election Day is just over one month away, providing an opportunity to review how markets have historically performed around midterm elections. For the full year, equity returns have historically been modest during midterm election years. Since 1970, the S&P 500 has generated an average total return of 3.6% during midterm election years, compared to an average annual return of 12.5% across all years from 1970–2025.* The two most recent midterm years were particularly challenging for stocks, with the index declining 18.1% in 2022 and 4.4% in 2018.* Stocks have bucked that historical pattern in 2026, however, with the S&P 500 up roughly 14% year to date including dividends, through yesterday's close. Looking ahead, the month immediately preceding midterm elections and the six months following Election Day have historically been favorable periods for the market. The S&P 500 has gained an average of 4.5% during the month leading up to Election Day, with positive returns in 78.6% of midterm election years.* Over the subsequent six months, the index has generated an average return of 15.5% and posted gains following all 14 midterm elections since 1970.* While there is no guarantee that history will repeat itself this election cycle, we believe these results help reinforce the importance of maintaining a disciplined investment strategy and resisting the temptation to play politics with your portfolio.
Brock Weimer, CFA

Happy Thursday. Breaking news this morning: Nvidia has agreed to buy open-source artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face
for nearly $13 billion.
Stock futures
are mixed this morning after a
winning day
on Wall Street.
Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day:
1. Summit up
The G20 wrapped up its two-day Innovation Ministerial yesterday, where technology leaders and government representatives talked artificial intelligence, data centers and tariffs.
Here are some of the biggest headlines out of the gathering:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said that AI will “democratize intelligence” for G20 countries and called the technology “the great equalizer.”
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, meanwhile, said using AI is a “non-negotiable” for countries, comparing the adoption of AI to the adoption of electricity.
Palantir CEO Alex Karp acknowledged that there are “huge dangers” to the technology but pushed back on what he called the “doom message” around AI. He appeared to allude to Anthropic and its CEO, who have warned about the technology’s risks.
On the data center front, Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown said he “really loved” President Donald Trump’s Monday Truth Social post, in which the president said communities who opposed data centers “want to end up being backwards and poor.”
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick said that data centers will “bring prosperity” and are “getting a bad rap.” He also downplayed the facilities’ water consumption.
Catch up on all the biggest moments here.
2. Bond, John Bond
After hitting its
highest level since 2023
, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield pulled back in Wednesday’s session, providing relief for other corners of the market.
New York Federal Reserve President John Williams told CNBC yesterday that the recent yield jumps should be seen as
a sign of a strong economy
rather than as market dysfunction. Williams also said he would have to “wait and see” before deciding whether an interest rate hike would be necessary to calm inflation.
The three major averages snapped three-day losing streaks yesterday.
Follow live market updates here.
3. Snow forecast
Snowflake soared 24%

Say it with us now: The most important thing for long-term stock growth is earnings.
Specifically, expectations and outlooks. We know we've harped on this for a long time, but we do that for a very good reason: It's uncontrovertibly true.
This also means that when those expectations turn, it's essentially as if the economy's Boeing 777 is having engine trouble.
Tracking equity analysts' revisions is a key measure of the market's directionality, and for the first time in months, there have been more stock downgrades than upgrades.
This happens plenty, even if the Citigroup US Earnings Revision Index hasn't been negative since April. But this run since April has been the longest bullish swing of upgrades in
